assistant.content:
Here’s a step-by-step framework you can follow to secure your Airbnb with cameras or sensors while fully respecting guest privacy and staying on the right side of both Airbnb policy and local law.

1. Check Airbnb Policy First  
 •   Airbnb prohibits any hidden or undisclosed recording devices anywhere on or in the property.  
 •   All cameras or other monitoring devices must be:  
     –   Visible (not concealed in smoke detectors, clocks, outlets, etc.)  
     –   Disclosed clearly in your listing (in both the “House Rules” and photos or description)  
 •   You may not place any device (camera, audio recorder, motion-activated audio, etc.) in private spaces—bedrooms or bathrooms—even if turned off or with audio disabled.

2. Understand Local & Federal Privacy Laws  
 •   In the U.S., the federal Electronic Communications Privacy Act (ECPA) generally bars audio recording without consent; many states (CA, FL, PA, WA, etc.) require two-party consent for audio.  
 •   Some jurisdictions treat hallways or shared corridors as “common areas” vs. private. When in doubt, treat every interior space as private.  
 •   If you’re in the EU or handle EU guests’ data, you must comply with the GDPR:  
     –   Establish a lawful basis (e.g., “legitimate interest” for property security)  
     –   Perform a short DPIA (data protection impact assessment)  
     –   Provide a concise privacy notice detailing what you record, why, retention period, and how guests can access/delete their data.

3. Limit Monitoring to Exterior & Common Areas Only  
 •   Outdoor cameras are acceptable if:  
     –   They point only at your own property (not neighbors’ yards or public sidewalks)  
     –   They do not capture audio  
     –   They are disclosed in your listing  
 •   If you have shared indoor common spaces (e.g. lobby of a multi-unit building), you may install visible cameras there—again, with full disclosure—but none in private areas (units, bedrooms, baths).

4. Do Not Record Audio  
 •   Video-only doorbells or cameras are strongly recommended.  
 •   If your hardware includes a mic, disable it in firmware/settings.  
 •   Always assume audio recording carries a higher legal risk.

5. Full Disclosure & Signage  
 •   In your Airbnb listing:  
     –   Add a “Security” section listing each device type (e.g., “Ring doorbell at front entry,” “Outdoor pan-tilt camera in backyard”)  
     –   Include a photo or icon of each device in the photo carousel  
 •   On-site signage (e.g. a small plaque by the front door) stating “Security cameras in operation” is good practice and, in some jurisdictions, legally required.

6. Secure Your Footage & Minimize Retention  
 •   Encryption: store video in an encrypted cloud or on a locked local DVR/NVR.  
 •   Access controls: restrict who can view/download footage—use strong, unique passwords and 2FA whenever possible.  
 •   Retention policy: keep footage only as long as necessary for security investigations (30 – 45 days is common), then delete automatically.

7. Consider Non-Video Alternatives for Indoor Security  
 •   Door/window contact sensors (notify you of forced entry)  
 •   Motion sensors without cameras (detect unexpected movement)  
 •   Smart deadbolts & keypads (audit logs of who enters/exits)  
 •   Smoke, CO and water-leak detectors  

8. Keep Documentation & Stay Up to Date  
 •   Maintain a simple log of:  
     –   What devices you have and where they’re installed  
     –   When you updated firmware or changed passwords  
 •   Periodically review your local regulations and Airbnb’s policy (they do change)  

Quick Checklist Before Your Next Guest Arrives  
 1.   All cameras visible and disclosed in your listing.  
 2.   No devices (camera or audio) in bedrooms or bathrooms.  
 3.   Audio disabled on any video hardware.  
 4.   Signage up at point of entry.  
 5.   Footage encrypted, access-limited, auto-deleted after ~30 days.  
 6.   Alternative non-video sensors in use indoors, if desired.  

By following these steps, you’ll deter vandalism or break-ins, have evidence if something goes wrong, but still honor your guests’ expectation of privacy—and keep your listing in good standing with both Airbnb and local regulators.
